title: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate · Units 43–44
description: Curated vocabulary for books, film genres and reviews, musical tastes, instruments, performers and recordings.

units.title: Unit 43 — Books and films
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 92–93 (PDF pages 93–94).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Recognise vocabulary for fiction, literary genres, authors and poems.
Contrast biographies and autobiographies, and relate poet, poetry and poem.
Talk about film genres, preferences, reviews and cinema listings.
Use natural collocations and word families for acting, entertainment, reviewing and directing.
Choose correct forms and complete short descriptions of books and films.

items.example: She enjoys studying literature at university.
items.note: Serious or artistically important writing, including novels and poetry.

items.example: I prefer fiction to books about real historical events.
items.note: Stories about invented people or events; an uncountable noun.

items.example: He is reading a long novel set in Scotland.
items.note: A book-length work of fiction; a countable noun.

items.pt: romance de suspense; filme de suspense
items.example: The thriller kept me guessing until the final chapter.
items.note: An exciting story, often involving danger or crime.

items.example: My favourite science fiction stories are about space travel.
items.note: Fiction dealing with imagined scientific developments or future worlds.

items.example: The author is visiting the bookshop to meet readers.
items.note: A person who writes a book or another written work.

items.example: I borrowed a biography of a famous scientist.
items.note: An account of someone's life written by another person; contrast with autobiography.

items.example: She likes reading poetry before going to bed.
items.note: Poems considered collectively; generally uncountable.

items.example: The poet read some of her work to the audience.
items.note: A person who writes poems.

items.example: He wrote a short poem about the sea.
items.note: An individual piece of writing in verse; a countable noun.

items.example: I started off with short stories before trying longer novels.
items.note: To begin a series or activity with a particular thing.

items.example: We watched a film at home after dinner.
items.note: British English normally uses film for a movie.

items.example: My brother refuses to watch a horror film on his own.
items.note: A film intended to frighten its audience.

items.example: The newspaper published a positive review of the new film.
items.note: An opinion or assessment of a film, book or performance; noun.

items.example: The film got good reviews, so we decided to see it.
items.note: A natural collocation for a film or book that critics praise.

items.example: A well-known star appears in the leading role.
items.note: A famous actor or performer; here it means a person, not an object in the sky.

items.example: The actor gave a convincing performance.
items.note: A person who performs a role in a film or play.

items.example: The plot was so complicated that I got confused.
items.note: Having many connected parts and being difficult to understand.

items.example: We go to the cinema mainly for entertainment.
items.note: Activities or experiences that people enjoy; generally uncountable.

items.example: The comedy made everyone in the room laugh.
items.note: A funny film or play; contrast with a horror film.

items.example: They chose a romantic comedy for their date.
items.note: A comedy whose story includes romance.

items.pt: o que está em cartaz; o que está passando
items.example: Let's check what's on at the cinema this weekend.
items.note: An informal way to ask which films or events are being shown.

items.pt: estar com vontade de assistir; querer ver
items.example: Do you fancy seeing a comedy tonight?
items.note: British informal English: fancy + -ing means want to do something.

items.pt: diretor de cinema; diretora de cinema
items.example: The film director worked closely with the actors.
items.note: The person responsible for the creative direction of a film.

items.example: Have you seen the director's latest film?
items.note: Latest means most recent, not necessarily best.

items.example: I listened to her latest interview yesterday.
items.note: Superlative adjective referring to the most recent one.

items.example: I am interested in films about history.
items.note: Use interested in + noun or -ing form.

items.example: The magician entertained the children for an hour.
items.note: Verb; related forms include entertainment and entertainer.

items.example: The entertainer told jokes and sang songs.
items.note: A person who entertains an audience.

items.example: She reviews new films for a local newspaper.
items.note: Verb: to write or give a critical opinion about something.

items.example: The reviewer praised the acting but disliked the ending.
items.note: A person who gives opinions about books, films or performances.

items.example: She wants to act in a school play.
items.note: To perform a role as an actor.

items.example: The acting was excellent even though the story was weak.
items.note: The work or skill of performing a role.

items.example: He hopes to direct a short film next year.
items.note: The verb direct means control the artistic making of a film.

items.example: She studied directing before making her first film.
items.note: The activity or art of directing films or plays.

items.example: The singer published an autobiography at the age of forty.
items.note: A story of a person's life written by that same person; contrast with biography.

items.example: This novel takes place in the nineteenth century.
items.note: A period of one hundred years; use century, not year, for a hundred-year period.

items.example: The television series is based on a popular novel.
items.note: Based on introduces the source material adapted for a film or programme.

items.example: The new film comes out next Friday.
items.note: Of films, books or albums: become available to the public; also taught explicitly for music in Unit 44.

items.example: Good comedies make people laugh without being cruel.
items.note: Make + person + base verb; contrast with horror films that frighten people.

sectionsChecked: A: Books including the literary genres and poet/poem forms
B: Films including the illustrated preference dialogues
Exercises 43.1–43.5 including crossword, corrections, word formation and film dialogue

units.title: Unit 44 — Music
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 94–95 (PDF pages 95–96).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Describe musical tastes, genres, live performances, tunes and lyrics.
Name illustrated musical instruments and the people who play them.
Explain the roles of composers, songwriters, conductors, orchestras and solo artists.
Describe recording, advertising, releasing and downloading albums and singles.
Use standard music collocations and distinguish classical music from classic music.

items.example: My musical taste has changed since I was a teenager.
items.note: The kinds of music someone likes.

items.example: My friends usually listen to pop music on the radio.
items.note: Popular contemporary music, often with short, catchy songs.

items.example: The festival includes traditional folk music.
items.note: Music connected with the traditions of a community.

items.example: She listens to classical music while she studies.
items.note: Say classical music, not classic music, for this genre.

items.example: We bought tickets for a concert on Saturday.
items.note: A live musical performance attended by an audience.

items.example: The band will perform at the festival tomorrow.
items.note: To sing, play music or entertain in front of people.

items.example: They perform live in small venues every month.
items.note: Live is pronounced /laɪv/ when it means in front of an audience.

items.example: Her live performance was even better than the recording.
items.note: A show taking place in front of an audience.

items.example: The orchestra gave a wonderful performance.
items.note: A particular occasion when someone performs.

items.example: The audience applauded at the end of the concert.
items.note: People watching or listening to a performance; a collective noun.

items.example: I remember the tune, but I have forgotten the words.
items.note: A sequence of musical notes that makes a melody.

items.example: The lyrics describe a journey away from home.
items.note: The words of a song; usually used in the plural.

items.example: Which musical instrument would you like to learn?
items.note: Something used to produce musical sounds.

items.example: The musician plays several different instruments.
items.note: A person who performs or makes music.

items.example: There is an old piano in the sitting room.
items.note: A large keyboard instrument with strings struck by hammers.

items.example: The pianist practises for two hours every morning.
items.note: A person who plays the piano.

items.example: She carries her cello in a large case.
items.note: A low-pitched string instrument played with a bow while seated.

items.example: The cellist played a beautiful solo.
items.note: A person who plays the cello.

items.example: He started learning the violin at primary school.
items.note: A small bowed string instrument.

items.example: The violinist joined the orchestra last year.
items.note: A person who plays the violin.

items.example: She learned three songs on the guitar.
items.note: A string instrument commonly played by strumming or plucking.

items.example: The guitarist performs with a jazz group.
items.note: A person who plays the guitar.

items.example: My cousin plays the saxophone in a band.
items.note: A wind instrument often heard in jazz and pop music.

items.example: The saxophonist played a short solo.
items.note: A person who plays the saxophone.

items.example: The trumpet sounded bright and clear.
items.note: A brass instrument played by blowing through a mouthpiece.

items.example: The trumpeter stood at the front of the stage.
items.note: A person who plays the trumpet.

items.example: We could hear the drums from outside the hall.
items.note: In a band, the drums form the percussion part.

items.example: The drummer kept a steady rhythm throughout the song.
items.note: A person who plays the drums.

items.example: She plays the bass guitar in a rock band.
items.note: A low-pitched electric string instrument; bass is pronounced /beɪs/.

items.example: The bass guitarist played alongside the drummer.
items.note: A musician who plays the bass guitar.

items.example: He chose the flute because he liked its soft sound.
items.note: A woodwind instrument played by blowing across an opening.

items.example: The flautist joined the school orchestra.
items.note: A person who plays the flute; the word flutist also exists.

items.example: Our band uses a keyboard for electronic sounds.
items.note: An electronic or acoustic instrument played with keys; context determines the meaning.

items.example: The keyboard player also writes songs.
items.note: A musician who plays the keyboard.

items.example: I want to learn to play the piano.
items.note: Use play + the + musical instrument in general statements.

items.example: The composer wrote music for several films.
items.note: A person who creates music, especially classical or instrumental music.

items.example: She plans to compose a short piece for the concert.
items.note: Verb related to composer; create music.

items.example: The songwriter writes the words and music for her songs.
items.note: A person who writes songs; unlike singer, this describes writing rather than performing.

items.example: The conductor raised her hands and the orchestra began.
items.note: A person who directs an orchestra or choir during a performance.

items.example: He will conduct the orchestra during the final piece.
items.note: Conduct is a verb pronounced /kənˈdʌkt/ in this meaning; it means lead musicians.

items.example: The orchestra has more than sixty musicians.
items.note: A large group playing different musical instruments together.

items.example: We watched an opera at the theatre last month.
items.note: A dramatic work in which most or all of the words are sung.

items.pt: cantor de ópera; cantora de ópera
items.example: The opera singer performed in several European theatres.
items.note: Someone who sings roles in opera.

items.example: The children went to see a ballet at Christmas.
items.note: An artistic dance performance, usually set to music.

items.pt: bailarino de balé; bailarina de balé
items.example: The ballet dancer rehearses every afternoon.
items.note: A performer who dances in ballet productions.

items.example: After leaving the band, she became a solo artist.
items.note: A singer or musician performing independently of a group.

items.example: The band is recording songs for its next album.
items.note: A group of musicians performing together, especially popular music.

items.example: Their group became popular after a television performance.
items.note: Group can mean a band in a music context.

items.example: The band's new album includes ten original songs.
items.note: A collection of recorded songs or pieces of music.

items.example: They will record their new song on Friday.
items.note: The verb record is pronounced /rɪˈkɔːd/; the noun record has first-syllable stress.

items.example: The singer released a single before the album.
items.note: A recording of one principal song, released separately.

items.example: We visited a recording studio during our trip.
items.note: A place with equipment for recording music or other audio.

items.example: The album comes out at the end of November.
items.note: An album or single comes out when it becomes available to the public.

items.example: The record label will advertise the concert online.
items.note: To tell people about a product or event through paid promotion.

items.example: The tour was advertised on television.
items.note: Past participle of advertise; often used in the passive voice.

items.example: I saw an advert for the festival on the train.
items.note: British English: a shortened form of advertisement.

items.pt: a mídia; os meios de comunicação
items.example: The media helped the young singer become famous.
items.note: Television, newspapers, radio and online channels collectively.

items.example: I prefer to download songs before travelling.
items.note: The verb download means copying digital content from the internet to a device.

items.example: The third track on the album is my favourite.
items.note: An individual song or piece of recorded music, not a sports track.

items.example: The rock guitarist played an energetic solo.
items.note: A guitarist who performs rock music; this combination occurs in the music quiz.

items.pt: single de sucesso; música de sucesso
items.example: Their first hit single reached the top of the charts.
items.note: A single that becomes popular or commercially successful.

items.pt: sucesso em primeiro lugar nas paradas
items.example: The song became a number one hit in several countries.
items.note: A recording that reaches the top of a music chart.

items.example: The lead singer introduced the band to the audience.
items.note: The main vocalist in a band or group.
